post.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

## Scenario context ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true glo… This walkthrough focuses on **The Write That Silently Disappeared**. Before making a design choice, clarify: - A payments team at a mid-size fintech company migrated their account ledger service from PostgreSQL to DynamoDB. - In PostgreSQL, every funds transfer ran inside a BEGIN / COMMIT block: debit the source account, credit the destination account, write a transaction record — three rows, one atomic commit. - The team ported the logic verbatim to DynamoDB and deployed. **Concepts in play:** transaction-isolation-distributed-acid, consistency-replication, event-driven-architecture, caching ## Stage 1 — ACID Unpacked for Distributed Systems: What Each Letter Means When There Is No Single Machine - The ACID acronym was coined for single-node relational databases. - Transplanted into distributed systems, each letter means something subtly different — and one of them barely means anything at all. - Atomicity in a distributed context means all writes in a logical transaction either all commit or all abort, even when those writes span multiple nodes, partitions, or shards. - On a single machine, "all or nothing" is enforced by the storage engine via write-ahead logging — a crash before the WAL is flushed is a rollback, a crash after is a commit. *Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "ACID Unpacked for Distributed Systems: What Each Letter Means When There Is No Single Machine - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` **Observable outcome:** On a single machine, "all or nothing" is enforced by the storage engine via write-ahead logging — a crash before the WAL is flushed is a rollback, a crash after is a commit. ## Stage 2 — DynamoDB TransactWriteItems: Two-Phase Commit Without Calling It Two-Phase Commit - Amazon DynamoDB added transactional APIs in late 2018 via TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems . - The documentation describes ACID guarantees for up to 25 items across up to 25 tables within a single AWS region. - What the documentation does not say is that these APIs implement a variant of two-phase commit backed by a coordinator item stored in DynamoDB's own infrastructure. - How the Coordinator Item Orchestrates 2PC When a client calls TransactWriteItems , DynamoDB's transaction layer writes a transaction record — a special metadata item tracked internally — with status PENDING and the full… *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Client participant Coordinator participant PartitionA as Partition A participant PartitionB as Partition B Client->>Coordinator: TransactWriteItems with ClientRequestToken Coordinator->>Coordinator: Write PENDING transaction record Coordinator->>PartitionA: PREPARE - lock item, evaluate condition, tentative write Coordinator->>PartitionB: PREPARE - lock item, evaluate condition, tentative write PartitionA-->>Coordinator: PREPARED PartitionB-->>Coordinator: PREPARED Coordinator->>Coordinator: Update transaction record to COMMITTED Coordinator->>PartitionA: COMMIT - apply write, release lock Coordinator->>PartitionB: COMMIT - apply write, release lock PartitionA-->>Coordinator: ACK PartitionB-->>Coordinator: ACK Coordinator-->>Client: TransactionSucceeded ``` **Observable outcome:** How the Coordinator Item Orchestrates 2PC When a client calls TransactWriteItems , DynamoDB's transaction layer writes a transaction record — a special metadata item tracked internally — with status PENDING and the full… ## Stage 3 — Cosmos DB Partition-Scoped Transactions: When JavaScript Is the Transaction Boundary - Azure Cosmos DB supports multi-document transactions, but under a constraint that surprises most developers: all documents in a transaction must share the same logical partition key . - There is no cross-partition atomic write in Cosmos DB. - Understanding why requires understanding what the transaction boundary actually is. - Stored Procedures as the Transaction Unit Cosmos DB's transaction boundary is the stored procedure execution . *Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.* ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Client sends stored procedure call] --> B{All document operations use same partition key?} B -->|No - different partition keys| C[Request rejected at routing layer] B -->|Yes| D[Route to owning partition primary replica] D --> E[Execute stored procedure JavaScript on primary] E --> F{JavaScript throws uncaught exception?} F -->|Yes| G[Engine rolls back all ops in this invocation] F -->|No| H[Commit - all mutations visible atomically] G --> I[Return error to client] H --> J[Return success to client] ``` **Observable outcome:** Stored Procedures as the Transaction Unit Cosmos DB's transaction boundary is the stored procedure execution . ## Stage 4 — Google Spanner and Global ACID: The Engineering Cost of External Consistency - Google Spanner is the only database in this comparison that delivers true global ACID transactions across any number of rows, tables, and geographic regions simultaneously. - This is not a marketing claim. - It is an engineering achievement built on physical infrastructure most databases do not have. - TrueTime: Bounding the Unknowable Every distributed database that uses timestamps for ordering faces the clock synchronization problem : two nodes' clocks can drift by milliseconds or more. *Applies **caching** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "Google Spanner and Global ACID: The Engineering Cost of External Consistency - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Client participant Leader as Spanner Partition Leader participant TrueTime as TrueTime API Client->>Leader: Begin read-write transaction Client->>Leader: Read rows R1, R2 - shared locks acquired Client->>Leader: Write mutations M1, M2 Leader->>Leader: Acquire exclusive write locks on M1, M2 Leader->>TrueTime: TT.now() - request current time interval TrueTime-->>Leader: Interval [t_earliest, t_latest] Note over Leader: Assign commit timestamp s = t_latest Leader->>Leader: Commit-wait - sleep until TT.now().t_earliest is greater than s Leader->>Leader: Apply writes atomically with timestamp s Leader->>Leader: Release all read and write locks Leader-->>Client: Commit ACK with timestamp s ``` **Observable outcome:** TrueTime: Bounding the Unknowable Every distributed database that uses timestamps for ordering faces the clock synchronization problem : two nodes' clocks can drift by milliseconds or more. ## Stage 5 — MongoDB Multi-Document Transactions: Oplog-Based Atomicity With a Sharding Caveat - MongoDB added multi-document transactions in version 4.0 for replica sets (2018) and extended them to sharded clusters in version 4.2 (2019). - MongoDB's transaction model builds on its existing replication infrastructure — the oplog (operations log) — and shares conceptual ancestry with Spanner's 2PC, though with higher overhead in the sharded case. - Replica Set Transactions: The Oplog as the Commit Record On a replica set, all read and write operations in a transaction execute on the primary node. - Reads use a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the data (MVCC-based), meaning reads inside a transaction never see commits from concurrent transactions — only data as it existed when the transaction began. *Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "MongoDB Multi-Document Transactions: Oplog-Based Atomicity With a Sharding Caveat - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` **Observable outcome:** Reads use a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the data (MVCC-based), meaning reads inside a transaction never see commits from concurrent transactions — only data as it existed when the transaction began. ## Stage 6 — Deep Dive: How Distributed ACID Is Actually Enforced Under the Hood - Understanding the mechanics of each database's transaction implementation requires examining three layers: the concurrency control model, the mathematical guarantees it formalizes, and the performance cost those guarant… - The Internals: Concurrency Control Models Compared Each database uses a different concurrency control strategy to achieve isolation, and that strategy determines both its failure modes under contention and its performan… - DynamoDB uses optimistic concurrency control (OCC) with condition expressions. - Rather than locking items during the transaction's lifetime, DynamoDB validates conditions at PREPARE time — atomically checking version numbers, attribute existence, or value predicates at the point of tentative write. *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "Deep Dive: How Distributed ACID Is Actually Enforced Under the Hood - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD DB["Database
(WAL/Log)"] Capture["Capture Engine"] Transform["Transform"] Sink["Sink/Destination"] DB -->|"Change Log"| Capture Capture -->|"CDC Event"| Transform Transform -->|"Normalized"| Sink ``` **Observable outcome:** Rather than locking items during the transaction's lifetime, DynamoDB validates conditions at PREPARE time — atomically checking version numbers, attribute existence, or value predicates at the point of tentative write. ## End-to-end outcome After working through the stages, you should be able to explain: - Two sequential writes are never a transaction. - The most common distributed transaction bug is issuing two independent write calls and assuming they are atomic because they run in the same Lambda or service method. ## Alternatives considered ### Isolation Levels Compared: Which Anomalies Each Database Prevents for Transactional Reads The following table maps each database's transactional API to its effective isolation level and the anomalies it prevents. ### Side-by-Side Comparison: Atomicity Scope, Isolation, Latency, and Cost Side-by-Side Comparison: Atomicity Scope, Isolation, Latency, and Cost ## Failure and degraded modes ### Trade-offs and Failure Modes Across All Four Databases - **Detection:** Performance versus correctness. - **User or operator impact:** Performance versus correctness.

footerPosts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
footerPosts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
footerPosts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

footerPosts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

footerPosts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
footerPosts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

footerPosts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
footerPosts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
footerPosts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

footerPosts.title: Apache Spark for Data Engineers: RDDs, DataFrames, and Structured Streaming
footerPosts.subtitle: Process petabytes with Python: understand Spark's execution model, DataFrame transformations, partitioning strategy, and real-time streaming.
footerPosts.brief: Apache Spark distributes Python DataFrame jobs across a cluster of executors, using lazy evaluation and the Catalyst query optimizer to process terabytes with the same code that works on gigabytes. Master partitioning, shuffle-awareness, and Structured Streaming and you have a single engine for both batch and real-time pipelines.

footerPosts.title: Attention Mechanism Explained: How Transformers Learn to Focus
footerPosts.subtitle: From the query-key-value formulation to multi-head attention — the mechanism that made transformers dominate AI
footerPosts.brief: Attention lets every token in a sequence ask "what else is relevant to me?" — dynamically weighting relationships across all positions simultaneously. It replaced the fixed-size hidden-state bottleneck of RNNs and is the engine behind every GPT, BERT, ViT, and AlphaFold model you have ever used.

footerPosts.title: API Gateway vs. Load Balancer vs. Reverse Proxy: What's the Difference?
footerPosts.subtitle: They all sit in front of your servers. But do you need Nginx, HAProxy, or Kong? We clarify the roles of each component.
footerPosts.brief: A **Reverse Proxy** hides your servers and handles caching/SSL. A **Load Balancer** spreads traffic across server instances. An **API Gateway** manages API concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, and protocol translation. Modern tools (Nginx, AWS ALB, Kong) often combine all three, but understanding what each layer does independently is essential for system design.

footerPosts.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF): Tailoring APIs for UI
footerPosts.subtitle: Mobile apps need less data than Desktop dashboards. Why serve them the same JSON? The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern solves this.
footerPosts.brief: A "one-size-fits-all" API causes bloated mobile payloads and underpowered desktop dashboards. The **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** pattern solves this by creating a dedicated API server for each client type — the mobile BFF reshapes data for small screens, the web BFF aggregates for dashboards.

footerPosts.title: BFS — Breadth-First Search: Level-by-Level Graph Exploration
footerPosts.subtitle: BFS explores graphs level by level using a queue — the key to shortest paths and level-order problems.
footerPosts.brief: BFS explores a graph level by level using a FIFO queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Recognize BFS problems by keywords: "shortest path," "minimum steps," or "level order." Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Mark nodes visited on enqueue — never on dequeue.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Backtracking Techniques in Data Structures
footerPosts.subtitle: Backtracking is a brute-force algorithmic technique that solves problems by trying to build a sol...
footerPosts.brief: Backtracking is "Recursion with Undo." You try a path, explore it deeply, and if it fails, you **undo** your last decision and try the next option. It explores the full search space but prunes invalid branches early, making it far more efficient than brute force.

footerPosts.title: Big Data Architecture Patterns: Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh
footerPosts.subtitle: Choose ingestion, serving, and ownership patterns deliberately when data platforms start to scale.
footerPosts.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

footerPosts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
footerPosts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
footerPosts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Different Types of Binary Trees
footerPosts.subtitle: Not all Binary Trees are created equal. We explain Full, Complete, Perfect, and Balanced Binary T...
footerPosts.brief: A Binary Tree has at most 2 children per node, but the **shape** of the tree determines performance. A **Full** tree has 0 or 2 children. A **Complete** tree fills left-to-right. A **Perfect** tree is a symmetric triangle. A **Degenerate** tree becomes a linked list with $O(N)$ search.

footerPosts.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
footerPosts.subtitle: Master Big O notation: measure algorithm efficiency from O(1) to O(n²) with growth diagrams, worked examples, and the interview mental model.
footerPosts.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

footerPosts.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
footerPosts.subtitle: Binary search has five distinct patterns — classic, leftmost, rightmost, rotated arrays, and 2D matrices.
footerPosts.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

morePosts.title: Azure Cosmos DB API Modes Explained: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, PostgreSQL, Gremlin, and Table
morePosts.subtitle: What each API can and cannot do — and the compatibility gaps that break production migrations
morePosts.brief: Cosmos DB's six API modes are wire-protocol compatibility layers over one shared ARS storage engine — except PostgreSQL (Citus), which is genuinely different. Every API emulates its native database incompletely, and those gaps are structural, not bugs. API mode is permanent and cannot be changed after account creation. NoSQL API is the only one with full Cosmos DB feature access. MongoDB API fails silently on complex aggregation pipelines. Cassandra API lacks materialized views and cross-partition transactions. PostgreSQL API is a managed Citus cluster — a different product entirely. Choose the right API before writing the first byte.

morePosts.title: Distributed Transactions: 2PC, Saga, and XA Explained
morePosts.subtitle: How to maintain data consistency across microservices when ACID transactions don't span databases.
morePosts.brief: Distributed transactions require you to choose a consistency model before choosing a protocol. 2PC and XA give atomic all-or-nothing commits but block all participants on coordinator failure. Saga gives eventual consistency with explicit compensation and survives coordinator crashes — at the cost of designing compensating transactions for every step. The Outbox pattern and idempotency are mandatory, not optional: they are what make Saga production-safe.

morePosts.title: Dirty Read Explained: How Uncommitted Data Corrupts Transactions
morePosts.subtitle: How a single uncommitted write can corrupt downstream reads, cause phantom transactions, and what isolation levels prevent it
morePosts.brief: A dirty read occurs when Transaction B reads data written by Transaction A before A has committed. If A rolls back, B has made decisions on data that never officially existed. Trace the anomaly from storage-engine visibility rules through multi-service fan-out and the isolation settings that close it.

morePosts.title: The Dual Write Problem in NoSQL: MongoDB, DynamoDB, and Cassandra
morePosts.subtitle: Why NoSQL consistency is harder than you think — and the per-database patterns that fix it
morePosts.brief: NoSQL databases trade cross-entity atomicity for scale — and every database draws that atomicity boundary in a different place. MongoDB's boundary is the document (pre-4.0) or the replica set (4.0+ multi-doc transactions). DynamoDB's boundary is a single `TransactWriteItems` call, with failure modes that silently burn throughput. Cassandra's boundary is the partition key. Write across any of these boundaries without a compensating pattern — Outbox, CDC, or conditional writes — and you will have silent data divergence in production.

moreArticles.subtitle: How to maintain data consistency across microservices when ACID transactions don't span databases.
moreArticles.brief: Distributed transactions require you to choose a consistency model before choosing a protocol. 2PC and XA give atomic all-or-nothing commits but block all participants on coordinator failure. Saga gives eventual consistency with explicit compensation and survives coordinator crashes — at the cost of designing compensating transactions for every step. The Outbox pattern and idempotency are mandatory, not optional: they are what make Saga production-safe.

moreArticles.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
moreArticles.subtitle: A deep dive into PostgreSQL WAL logs, MVCC snapshot isolation, Write Skew anomalies, and crash recovery
moreArticles.brief: Trace how storage engines process high-stakes financial transactions like bank transfers using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), and SSI locks without data loss or corruption.

moreArticles.title: Dirty Read Explained: How Uncommitted Data Corrupts Transactions
moreArticles.subtitle: How a single uncommitted write can corrupt downstream reads, cause phantom transactions, and what isolation levels prevent it
moreArticles.brief: A dirty read occurs when Transaction B reads data written by Transaction A before A has committed. If A rolls back, B has made decisions on data that never officially existed. Trace the anomaly from storage-engine visibility rules through multi-service fan-out and the isolation settings that close it.

moreArticles.title: The Dual Write Problem in NoSQL: MongoDB, DynamoDB, and Cassandra
moreArticles.subtitle: Why NoSQL consistency is harder than you think — and the per-database patterns that fix it
moreArticles.brief: NoSQL databases trade cross-entity atomicity for scale — and every database draws that atomicity boundary in a different place. MongoDB's boundary is the document (pre-4.0) or the replica set (4.0+ multi-doc transactions). DynamoDB's boundary is a single `TransactWriteItems` call, with failure modes that silently burn throughput. Cassandra's boundary is the partition key. Write across any of these boundaries without a compensating pattern — Outbox, CDC, or conditional writes — and you will have silent data divergence in production.

lmsArticle.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

## Scenario context ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true glo… This walkthrough focuses on **The Write That Silently Disappeared**. Before making a design choice, clarify: - A payments team at a mid-size fintech company migrated their account ledger service from PostgreSQL to DynamoDB. - In PostgreSQL, every funds transfer ran inside a BEGIN / COMMIT block: debit the source account, credit the destination account, write a transaction record — three rows, one atomic commit. - The team ported the logic verbatim to DynamoDB and deployed. **Concepts in play:** transaction-isolation-distributed-acid, consistency-replication, event-driven-architecture, caching ## Stage 1 — ACID Unpacked for Distributed Systems: What Each Letter Means When There Is No Single Machine - The ACID acronym was coined for single-node relational databases. - Transplanted into distributed systems, each letter means something subtly different — and one of them barely means anything at all. - Atomicity in a distributed context means all writes in a logical transaction either all commit or all abort, even when those writes span multiple nodes, partitions, or shards. - On a single machine, "all or nothing" is enforced by the storage engine via write-ahead logging — a crash before the WAL is flushed is a rollback, a crash after is a commit. *Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "ACID Unpacked for Distributed Systems: What Each Letter Means When There Is No Single Machine - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` **Observable outcome:** On a single machine, "all or nothing" is enforced by the storage engine via write-ahead logging — a crash before the WAL is flushed is a rollback, a crash after is a commit. ## Stage 2 — DynamoDB TransactWriteItems: Two-Phase Commit Without Calling It Two-Phase Commit - Amazon DynamoDB added transactional APIs in late 2018 via TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems . - The documentation describes ACID guarantees for up to 25 items across up to 25 tables within a single AWS region. - What the documentation does not say is that these APIs implement a variant of two-phase commit backed by a coordinator item stored in DynamoDB's own infrastructure. - How the Coordinator Item Orchestrates 2PC When a client calls TransactWriteItems , DynamoDB's transaction layer writes a transaction record — a special metadata item tracked internally — with status PENDING and the full… *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Client participant Coordinator participant PartitionA as Partition A participant PartitionB as Partition B Client->>Coordinator: TransactWriteItems with ClientRequestToken Coordinator->>Coordinator: Write PENDING transaction record Coordinator->>PartitionA: PREPARE - lock item, evaluate condition, tentative write Coordinator->>PartitionB: PREPARE - lock item, evaluate condition, tentative write PartitionA-->>Coordinator: PREPARED PartitionB-->>Coordinator: PREPARED Coordinator->>Coordinator: Update transaction record to COMMITTED Coordinator->>PartitionA: COMMIT - apply write, release lock Coordinator->>PartitionB: COMMIT - apply write, release lock PartitionA-->>Coordinator: ACK PartitionB-->>Coordinator: ACK Coordinator-->>Client: TransactionSucceeded ``` **Observable outcome:** How the Coordinator Item Orchestrates 2PC When a client calls TransactWriteItems , DynamoDB's transaction layer writes a transaction record — a special metadata item tracked internally — with status PENDING and the full… ## Stage 3 — Cosmos DB Partition-Scoped Transactions: When JavaScript Is the Transaction Boundary - Azure Cosmos DB supports multi-document transactions, but under a constraint that surprises most developers: all documents in a transaction must share the same logical partition key . - There is no cross-partition atomic write in Cosmos DB. - Understanding why requires understanding what the transaction boundary actually is. - Stored Procedures as the Transaction Unit Cosmos DB's transaction boundary is the stored procedure execution . *Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.* ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Client sends stored procedure call] --> B{All document operations use same partition key?} B -->|No - different partition keys| C[Request rejected at routing layer] B -->|Yes| D[Route to owning partition primary replica] D --> E[Execute stored procedure JavaScript on primary] E --> F{JavaScript throws uncaught exception?} F -->|Yes| G[Engine rolls back all ops in this invocation] F -->|No| H[Commit - all mutations visible atomically] G --> I[Return error to client] H --> J[Return success to client] ``` **Observable outcome:** Stored Procedures as the Transaction Unit Cosmos DB's transaction boundary is the stored procedure execution . ## Stage 4 — Google Spanner and Global ACID: The Engineering Cost of External Consistency - Google Spanner is the only database in this comparison that delivers true global ACID transactions across any number of rows, tables, and geographic regions simultaneously. - This is not a marketing claim. - It is an engineering achievement built on physical infrastructure most databases do not have. - TrueTime: Bounding the Unknowable Every distributed database that uses timestamps for ordering faces the clock synchronization problem : two nodes' clocks can drift by milliseconds or more. *Applies **caching** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "Google Spanner and Global ACID: The Engineering Cost of External Consistency - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Client participant Leader as Spanner Partition Leader participant TrueTime as TrueTime API Client->>Leader: Begin read-write transaction Client->>Leader: Read rows R1, R2 - shared locks acquired Client->>Leader: Write mutations M1, M2 Leader->>Leader: Acquire exclusive write locks on M1, M2 Leader->>TrueTime: TT.now() - request current time interval TrueTime-->>Leader: Interval [t_earliest, t_latest] Note over Leader: Assign commit timestamp s = t_latest Leader->>Leader: Commit-wait - sleep until TT.now().t_earliest is greater than s Leader->>Leader: Apply writes atomically with timestamp s Leader->>Leader: Release all read and write locks Leader-->>Client: Commit ACK with timestamp s ``` **Observable outcome:** TrueTime: Bounding the Unknowable Every distributed database that uses timestamps for ordering faces the clock synchronization problem : two nodes' clocks can drift by milliseconds or more. ## Stage 5 — MongoDB Multi-Document Transactions: Oplog-Based Atomicity With a Sharding Caveat - MongoDB added multi-document transactions in version 4.0 for replica sets (2018) and extended them to sharded clusters in version 4.2 (2019). - MongoDB's transaction model builds on its existing replication infrastructure — the oplog (operations log) — and shares conceptual ancestry with Spanner's 2PC, though with higher overhead in the sharded case. - Replica Set Transactions: The Oplog as the Commit Record On a replica set, all read and write operations in a transaction execute on the primary node. - Reads use a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the data (MVCC-based), meaning reads inside a transaction never see commits from concurrent transactions — only data as it existed when the transaction began. *Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "MongoDB Multi-Document Transactions: Oplog-Based Atomicity With a Sharding Caveat - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` **Observable outcome:** Reads use a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the data (MVCC-based), meaning reads inside a transaction never see commits from concurrent transactions — only data as it existed when the transaction began. ## Stage 6 — Deep Dive: How Distributed ACID Is Actually Enforced Under the Hood - Understanding the mechanics of each database's transaction implementation requires examining three layers: the concurrency control model, the mathematical guarantees it formalizes, and the performance cost those guarant… - The Internals: Concurrency Control Models Compared Each database uses a different concurrency control strategy to achieve isolation, and that strategy determines both its failure modes under contention and its performan… - DynamoDB uses optimistic concurrency control (OCC) with condition expressions. - Rather than locking items during the transaction's lifetime, DynamoDB validates conditions at PREPARE time — atomically checking version numbers, attribute existence, or value predicates at the point of tentative write. *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "Deep Dive: How Distributed ACID Is Actually Enforced Under the Hood - Storage Topology", "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.", "view": "data-flow", "pattern": "cache-aside", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" }, { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" }, { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" }, { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" }, { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Storage Access Pattern", "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications." } } ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD DB["Database
(WAL/Log)"] Capture["Capture Engine"] Transform["Transform"] Sink["Sink/Destination"] DB -->|"Change Log"| Capture Capture -->|"CDC Event"| Transform Transform -->|"Normalized"| Sink ``` **Observable outcome:** Rather than locking items during the transaction's lifetime, DynamoDB validates conditions at PREPARE time — atomically checking version numbers, attribute existence, or value predicates at the point of tentative write. ## End-to-end outcome After working through the stages, you should be able to explain: - Two sequential writes are never a transaction. - The most common distributed transaction bug is issuing two independent write calls and assuming they are atomic because they run in the same Lambda or service method. ## Alternatives considered ### Isolation Levels Compared: Which Anomalies Each Database Prevents for Transactional Reads The following table maps each database's transactional API to its effective isolation level and the anomalies it prevents. ### Side-by-Side Comparison: Atomicity Scope, Isolation, Latency, and Cost Side-by-Side Comparison: Atomicity Scope, Isolation, Latency, and Cost ## Failure and degraded modes ### Trade-offs and Failure Modes Across All Four Databases - **Detection:** Performance versus correctness. - **User or operator impact:** Performance versus correctness.

Replica Set Transactions: The Oplog as the Commit Record On a replica set, all read and write operations in a transaction execute on the primary node. - Reads use a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the data (MVCC-based), meaning reads inside a transaction never see commits from concurrent transactions — only data as it existed when the transaction began. *Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "MongoDB Multi-Document Transactions: Oplog-Based Atomicity With a Sharding Caveat - Understanding the mechanics of each database's transaction implementation requires examining three layers: the concurrency control model, the mathematical guarantees it formalizes, and the performance cost those guarant… - The Internals: Concurrency Control Models Compared Each database uses a different concurrency control strategy to achieve isolation, and that strategy determines both its failure modes under contention and its performan… - DynamoDB uses optimistic concurrency control (OCC) with condition expressions. - Rather than locking items during the transaction's lifetime, DynamoDB validates conditions at PREPARE time — atomically checking version numbers, attribute existence, or value predicates at the point of tentative write. *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "Deep Dive: How Distributed ACID Is Actually Enforced Under the Hood - (WAL/Log)"] Capture["Capture Engine"] Transform["Transform"] Sink["Sink/Destination"] DB -->|"Change Log"| Capture Capture -->|"CDC Event"| Transform Transform -->|"Normalized"| Sink ``` **Observable outcome:** Rather than locking items during the transaction's lifetime, DynamoDB validates conditions at PREPARE time — atomically checking version numbers, attribute existence, or value predicates at the point of tentative write. ## End-to-end outcome After working through the stages, you should be able to explain: - Two sequential writes are never a transaction. - The most common distributed transaction bug is issuing two independent write calls and assuming they are atomic because they run in the same Lambda or service method. ## Alternatives considered ### Isolation Levels Compared: Which Anomalies Each Database Prevents for Transactional Reads The following table maps each database's transactional API to its effective isolation level and the anomalies it prevents. ### Side-by-Side Comparison: Atomicity Scope, Isolation, Latency, and Cost Side-by-Side Comparison: Atomicity Scope, Isolation, Latency, and Cost ## Failure and degraded modes ### Trade-offs and Failure Modes Across All Four Databases - **Detection:** Performance versus correctness. - **User or operator impact:** Performance versus correctness.

stages.title: Stage 1 — ACID Unpacked for Distributed Systems: What Each Letter Means When There Is No Single Machine
stages.decisionOrAction: The ACID acronym was coined for single-node relational databases.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Governs the design decision for “ACID Unpacked for Distributed Systems: What Each Letter Means When There Is No Single Machine” in this scenario.

stages.componentBehavior: Transplanted into distributed systems, each letter means something subtly different — and one of them barely means anything at all.
stages.observableOutput: Atomicity in a distributed context means all writes in a logical transaction either all commit or all abort, even when those writes span multiple nodes, partitions, or shards.

stages.title: Stage 2 — DynamoDB TransactWriteItems: Two-Phase Commit Without Calling It Two-Phase Commit
stages.decisionOrAction: Amazon DynamoDB added transactional APIs in late 2018 via TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems .

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Governs the design decision for “DynamoDB TransactWriteItems: Two-Phase Commit Without Calling It Two-Phase Commit” in this scenario.

stages.componentBehavior: The documentation describes ACID guarantees for up to 25 items across up to 25 tables within a single AWS region.
stages.observableOutput: What the documentation does not say is that these APIs implement a variant of two-phase commit backed by a coordinator item stored in DynamoDB's own infrastructure.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Cosmos DB Partition-Scoped Transactions: When JavaScript Is the Transaction Boundary
stages.decisionOrAction: Azure Cosmos DB supports multi-document transactions, but under a constraint that surprises most developers: all documents in a transaction must share the same logical partition key .

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Governs the design decision for “Cosmos DB Partition-Scoped Transactions: When JavaScript Is the Transaction Boundary” in this scenario.

stages.componentBehavior: There is no cross-partition atomic write in Cosmos DB.
stages.observableOutput: Understanding why requires understanding what the transaction boundary actually is.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Google Spanner and Global ACID: The Engineering Cost of External Consistency
stages.decisionOrAction: Google Spanner is the only database in this comparison that delivers true global ACID transactions across any number of rows, tables, and geographic regions simultaneously.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Governs the design decision for “Google Spanner and Global ACID: The Engineering Cost of External Consistency” in this scenario.

stages.componentBehavior: This is not a marketing claim.
stages.observableOutput: It is an engineering achievement built on physical infrastructure most databases do not have.

useCase.goal: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal.
requirements: TLDR: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal.
DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region.
Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee.
constraints: Every strong isolation guarantee costs latency.
assumptions: Illustrative teaching scenario. Claims remain pending editorial review before publication.
